sections.title: What every professional electrician invoice must show
sections.body: A generic invoice template fails because electrical work involves distinct billing elements. Your invoice must clearly separate your initial call-out fee from the actual hourly labour. Clients need to see exactly what parts you supplied, from consumer units to simple switches, and the price applied to each. If you performed safety testing or issued an electrical installation certificate, this must appear as a separate line item. Finally, you should always include your warranty terms at the bottom of the document. Stating that labour is guaranteed for twelve months but parts are subject to manufacturer warranties prevents future arguments.
items: A clear separation between call-out fees and hourly labour rates.
Itemised lists of all supplied materials like wire and breakers.
Specific line items for safety testing and compliance certificates.
Clear warranty terms for both parts and installation labour.

sections.title: How electrical jobs are priced and billed
sections.body: Electricians typically bill using a mix of fixed fees, hourly rates, and material markups. For domestic repairs, you might charge a fixed call-out fee that covers the first hour of diagnostics, followed by a standard hourly rate. Emergency call-outs at night or on weekends require a higher out-of-hours rate. For materials, electricians purchase supplies at trade prices and apply a markup to cover sourcing and handling. When pricing larger commercial installations, you might quote a fixed project price, but the final invoice still needs to break down the stages of first fix and second fix wiring.
items: Standard hourly rates for routine domestic and commercial electrical work.
Premium out-of-hours rates for emergency fault finding and repairs.
Materials billed at cost plus a percentage markup for handling.
Fixed price stages for first fix and second fix installations.

sections.title: Managing deposits, payment terms, and chasing clients
sections.body: Cash flow is critical when you are buying expensive materials like copper wire and distribution boards upfront. For large rewiring projects, always invoice for a deposit before purchasing materials. Specify your payment terms clearly, such as payment due upon completion for domestic repairs, or thirty days for commercial contractors. If a client delays payment, you need a system to follow up. faqs.q: How do I bill for an electrical call-out fee?
faqs.a: A call-out fee should be listed as the very first item on your invoice. You should clearly state whether this fee includes the first hour of diagnostic work or if it is strictly a fee for arriving at the property. By separating this from your standard hourly labour rate, clients understand exactly what they are paying for before the repair work even begins.

faqs.q: Should I mark up the cost of electrical materials?
faqs.a: Yes, it is standard practice for electricians to apply a markup to materials like cables, sockets, and consumer units. This markup covers your time spent driving to the wholesaler, sourcing the correct parts, and handling the materials. You can list the final retail price on the invoice without showing the client your wholesale trade cost, ensuring your profit margin remains protected.

faqs.q: How do I invoice for emergency out-of-hours electrical work?
faqs.a: Emergency work should be billed at a higher rate than your standard daytime labour. Create a specific line item called 'Emergency Call-Out' or 'Out-of-Hours Labour' on your invoice. This transparency shows the client why the bill is higher than a routine daytime appointment. Always agree on this premium rate with the homeowner or site manager over the phone before you travel to the job.

faqs.q: Where should I put my warranty terms on the invoice?
faqs.a: Your warranty terms belong in the notes or terms section at the bottom of the invoice. You must be specific about what is covered. For example, state that your installation labour is guaranteed for twelve months, but the supplied electrical components are subject to the manufacturer's own warranty. Clear terms prevent disputes if a part fails six months after the installation.
